moments.title: Why the Mishnah names the Tanna
The power of a tzaddik's name
A name is the neshamah
Losing a name: Zimri and Dasan
What are the 'many things'?
Wine, Olam Haba and the power of a look
The whole world is worthwhile for him
Everything happens for the tzaddikim
Mitzvos bring down blessing
Loving Hashem and loved by people
No self-interest, no machlokes
Kept from sin: the Beis Halevi and Yeshuos Yaakov
The Vitebsker's fish in Eretz Yisrael
Food that once had a shaylah
The Slonimer Rebbe and the beard
Mr. Singer and the Radziner gabbai
A tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah raises himself until his name is Torah, so the Mishnah names him and mentioning his name is like saying words of Torah.
A tzaddik's name, and even the name of the place where he lived, carries his kedushah and can draw down a yeshuah for the one who mentions it.
The reward of one who learns Torah lishmah is so great that not even a navi saw it, and the whole world is worthwhile for him alone.
Everything that happens in the world, great or small, happens for the sake of the tzaddikim and Klal Yisrael, even when nobody knows why.
Mitzvos rise to Heaven and come down as blessing, aveiros come down as suffering, and the greatest blessing comes from Torah lishmah.
The one who learns lishmah has no interest of his own, so he loves Hashem and people alike and is loved by both.
The Torah he learns keeps him far from sin: Hashem gives such tzaddikim a special sense that warns them away from forbidden food.
The Mishnah names its Tannaim not only to know who said what: a tzaddik who learns lishmah becomes so holy that his very name is Torah, so saying 'Rabbi Akiva' is like saying a word of Torah.

A name in loshon hakodesh is the creature's essence: Adam saw from each animal's nature which letters it was made of, and a sinner loses his name, which is why Zimri and Cozbi are named only after Pinchas killed them.
The holier a thing is, the more easily it is spoiled; wine, which stands for the reward of Olam Haba, is spoiled even by a gentile's look, showing how holy that reward is.
World events like Vashti's death or Nixon's resignation are reported with worldly reasons, but their true cause is the tzaddikim and Klal Yisrael, which will become clear only when Mashiach comes.
The heavenly calls to teshuvah go out every day, and the receiver that picks them up is a Jewish heart; a sudden urge to do teshuvah is the heart catching one of them.
Machlokes comes from each person's private interests; one who learns lishmah has none, which is why he can love everyone, as all will in the days of Mashiach.
Loving a fellow Jew does not divide one's love of Hashem, since every Jew's neshamah is a part of Hashem; this is why 'love your fellow as yourself' ends with 'I am Hashem'.
Why does the Mishnah mention the Tanna's name when no one disputes him?
Why does the passuk not name the man and the Midianite woman during the sin, but names them after they were killed?
What are the 'many things' that one who learns Torah lishmah merits, if not the list the Tanna gives?
Why is wine spoiled so easily, even by a gentile's look?
Why does Hashem keep up a world so full of reshaim with so few tzaddikim?
How can a person love both Hashem and a fellow Jew without dividing his love?

The Rav says that when a person needs a yeshuah he should mention the names of tzaddikim, which brings kedushah upon him.
The Rav says a person should guard and strengthen his name and sanctify it, so that mentioning it will bring down blessing.
The Rav says that at hagbah everyone should look at the letters of the Sefer Torah and become holier from it.
Favor or righteousness; Cheshvan after Tishrei
Cheshvan's combination of Hashem's Name
Bringing Tishrei's honey into the month of Bul
Zichronos: why Noach needed to be remembered
The lion that wounded Noach
Could Noach have brought meat?
When Mashiach comes: the lion will eat straw
Man's deeds rule creation; Noach's portion
The Teivah as a sanctuary and a utopia
Why the lion eats meat; Cham's sin
Digression on the curse of Cham
The utopia lost, and Hashem's love for Noach
Encouragement for Cheshvan: the third world
Cheshvan, the month of Bul, of withering and decay, follows Tishrei, and the Rav says the sweetness and renewal of Tishrei must be carried into it.
In the Zichronos of Rosh Hashanah we recall that Hashem remembered Noach with love, and the Rav asks why that love was needed when the whole rescue had been planned in advance.
Man stands at the control center of creation: the sins of the generation of the Mabul were mirrored in the animals and even in the soil, while the part of creation under Noach stayed pure.
The Teivah was a place of kedushah like the world before Adam's sin, and there the lion did not need meat.
Cham's sin in the Teivah brought back the curse, the lion needed meat and wounded Noach, yet Hashem remembered Noach with love because Avraham and the Jewish people would come from him.

Cheshvan's combination of Hashem's Name is the only one drawn across two pesukim, from 'u'dvash' that ends a passage into 'hayom hazeh' that opens a new one, teaching that the honey of Tishrei must be carried over into the month of decay.
'Av HaRachaman', the merciful Father, has the gematria of 'dvash', honey, 306: in Tishrei Hashem appears to us as sweetness.

Every person governs his own portion of creation; Noach's portion was the animals that came into the Teivah, which stayed pure amid a corrupt world, and geographically Eretz Yisrael, where no Mabul fell.
The Teivah, built with halachos to exact dimensions like the Mishkan, was not a ship but a place of kedushah, an embassy of heaven on earth, and so the Mabul's law of destruction did not apply to it.

Life in food is the word of Hashem; the purer a creature, the more it extracts from less, so the tzaddik eats little and the sheep lives on grass, while the cruel lion must eat concentrated food, meat.
The lion's attack on Noach was a result of Cham's sin, which repeated Adam's sin inside the Teivah, brought back the curse and made the lion need meat again.
Hashem makes three tries: the worlds of Adam and of Noach were spoiled, and the third world, like the third Beis HaMikdash, will be perfect.
Why is Cheshvan's combination of Hashem's Name the only one drawn from the end of one passuk and the start of another?
Why did Hashem need to remember Noach with love when the whole rescue was planned in advance?
Why were the animals destroyed in the Mabul if they have no free choice?
Why does the lion eat meat, and why are carnivorous animals forbidden to eat?
If Noach could have brought preserved meat, and Hashem helped him with everything, why did he fail to feed the lion?
Rav Nachum of Chernobyl and his little bread
The Rav says one should not lose the renewal and resolutions gained in Tishrei, but carry them into Cheshvan so that the Torah feels new every day.
The Rav says that in Cheshvan, though one is not satisfied with what Tishrei achieved, one finds encouragement in Parshas Noach, which ends with the birth of Avraham Avinu.
Rain in the sukkah: the Rambam's limit
The sukkah as one's address
The first night fixes the dwelling
Chava's creation, renewed every Tishrei
Erusin and nisuin
Souls already joined; lost item and find
Adam and Chava began with nisuin
Knesses Yisrael's Tishrei, and the Satan's bone
Servant and son; holiness kept hidden
Moshiach comes concealed: Peretz and Zerach
This year's rain; from broken luchos to Bereishis
Words to the yeshiva
According to the Rav, rain is a bad sign only on the first night of Sukkos, because only then is there an obligation to eat in the sukkah; on other days a person has a choice.
The mitzvah of sukkah is to dwell there; like an address, the sukkah stays one's home even when rain sends him out.
The kezayis eaten on the first night establishes the sukkah as one's dwelling for all seven days, a stronger fixing than the meal placed for an eruv.
The creation of Chava and her coming to Adam repeats every year between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, from Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres.
Nisuin is a closer bond than erusin, yet its punishment is lighter, because it comes from the attribute of chesed.
The rain on Sukkos is the Satan's share at a time of great holiness, and a sign that a year of union with Hashem is approaching.
The breaking of the luchos is joined to Bereishis: after a broken Sukkos one can begin again.
The Rav reads the Rambam's limit as a matter of choice: a bad sign is only where a person had no choice, and only the first night of Sukkos obliges him to eat in the sukkah.
Leaving the sukkah for rain does not end one's dwelling there, just as a man's home address does not change when he steps out; therefore the exemption of one who suffers fits the mitzvah of dwelling.
An eruv is fixed for one day by placing a meal, but the sukkah must be fixed as a home for seven days, which needs an actual eating on the first night; this is why the kezayis is learned from matzah.

Tishrei is the yearly rebuilding of Chava for Adam: Rosh Hashanah as back to back, the shofar breaking through judgment, Yom Kippur as the separation, the sukkah as chuppah, and Shemini Atzeres as 'He brought her to the man'.
The Rav applies the Ramban's rule, that what comes from love carries a lighter punishment, to explain why a nesuah is punished by strangling while an arusah is stoned.
The missing heh in the Torah's word for a young woman points to what she lacks until nisuin, when she receives the heh and is raised to be one with her husband.
The breaking of the luchos at the end of the Torah is joined to its first word, Bereishis, which holds everything like a seed; so a broken Sukkos becomes a new beginning.
Why does the Rambam say the bad sign of rain applies only at the start of the festival?
Why is one who suffers in the sukkah exempt from it?
Why must one eat a kezayis in the sukkah on the first night?
Why is the nesuah, more closely bound to her husband, punished more lightly than the arusah?
The Rav expresses the hope that everyone hold firm together to emunah in the coming of Moshiach, even when a Jew does not understand what he sees.
The Rav teaches that after a broken Sukkos one can start again from Bereishis.
The Rav asks the older bochurim of the yeshiva to give of their time to help the younger ones.
Elul, the days of favor and the second luchos
Shmitah and the beloved seventh
Releasing others' debts before Rosh Hashanah
Letzanus, the opposite of emunah
Scoffers shut out of the palaces of tefillah
Pharaoh the scoffer
Pharaoh's punishment, measure for measure
Rosh Hashanah as a day of emes
Elul and Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael
The forty days of Elul were days of favor, and the teshuvah Klal Yisrael did then left a lasting mark on the season for all generations.
Shmitah means letting go; when a person releases what others owe him, Hashem correspondingly releases the debt of his sins.
Elul calls for strengthening one another in serving Hashem, and letzanus is what most cools a person's Yiddishkeit.
Following Rabbi Tzadok, emunah is the root and entrance of all good and letzanus is the root of all bad and the entrance to the opposite.
A scoffer is pushed away from the palaces of tefillah and loses his connection to davening and learning.
Pharaoh withstood the plagues because, as a scoffer, he used jokes to escape reality, and Hashem punished him measure for measure by making sport of Egypt.
The Rav reads 'shmitah to Hashem' as a mirror: by letting go of the debts others owe us, we cause Hashem to let go of the debt our sins have created.
Because the shmitah of years is counted from Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah is itself a time of release, and every Shabbos, the seventh day, is a small Rosh Hashanah with the same power.
Letzanus is the exact opposite of emunah: emunah is the gate into serving Hashem, and letzanus is the gate out of it.

Following Rabbi Tzadok, the Gemara's statement that scoffers do not receive the Shechinah means that the scoffer is kept out of the palaces of tefillah, so that even while davening his mind wanders elsewhere.
Pharaoh's superhuman stubbornness through the plagues came from his humor: a joke lets a person escape reality, so he never has to face it.
Pharaoh's punishment, 'that I made sport of Egypt', was measure for measure: Hashem let him make good jokes and then made a joke of him.
Why does the count of shmitah years begin from Tishrei?
What does the Gemara mean that scoffers do not receive the presence of the Shechinah?
Where does one see that Pharaoh was a scoffer, and how could a logical man withstand plague after plague?
What was Pharaoh's punishment for his scoffing?
The Ba'al Shem Tov greets a man after davening
The child who did not like fish
The Rav says that before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur one must be mochel others, letting go of what they owe, so that Hashem will let go of one's own debt.
The Rav says that the davening of this time should begin by accepting the mitzvah of loving one's fellow as oneself.
The Rav says one must strengthen others in serving Hashem and never cool them off with scoffing.
The week of yiras Hashem and the start of teshuvah
A shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael
Gap in the recording
Choosing right after Yom Kippur: the man from Biala
Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av
Av, Yerushalayim and a fear born of wholeness
Why avodah in galus is so precious
The two sides of Tisha b'Av
Rejoicing and making a reckoning
Adding in Torah from Chamishah Asar b'Av
Chamishah Asar b'Av is a time to draw yiras shamayim, falling in the week of parshas Eikev, the week of fear of Hashem among the seven weeks of comfort, and it opens the days of teshuvah.
The day of shidduchim is a shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and its tenaim are the passuk 'What does Hashem ask of you, but to fear Hashem… and to love Him'.
Yom Kippur makes a person free of sin, so his choice is good, and since the process of Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av, that day too is a time when a Jew's choice is at its best.

Since the churban, the avodah of Jews in galus is more precious to Hashem than the avodah of the great tzaddikim of the Beis Hamikdash era, as the Pesikta teaches on 'the children of the desolate are more than the children of the married one'.

On Chamishah Asar b'Av, rising from the mourning of Tisha b'Av, one rejoices that our avodah is precious, makes a reckoning that the opportunity may end when Moshiach comes, and adds in Torah, tefillah and Yiddishkeit.

The 'shidduch' of Chamishah Asar b'Av is between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the tenaim one must look over before the match are the passuk of parshas Eikev: to fear Hashem, walk in His ways and love Him.
Since teshuvah begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av and ends on Yom Kippur, and the end is embedded in the beginning, the good choice a Jew has on Yom Kippur is already present on Chamishah Asar b'Av.
Yerushalayim is 'yirah shleimah': holy fear of Hashem flows from wholeness, unlike ordinary fear, which comes from a person's lack, as one fears a lion because he lacks its strength.

Tisha b'Av contains two opposites, the churban and the gain that our avodah became more precious; the gain cannot be celebrated on Tisha b'Av itself, so Chamishah Asar b'Av, when the mourning ends, was set as its yom tov.

Because 'every generation in whose days the Beis Hamikdash is not rebuilt' suffers a new churban, each year's avodah is more precious than the last, which is why the Gemara says to add in learning from Chamishah Asar b'Av.
How did the man from Biala always end up with the finest choice?
How could the Arizal tell R' Chaim Vital that he was greater than earlier giants whose level he could not approach?
Why make a yom tov when a period of mourning ends, which is done nowhere else?
If galus is better for us, why do we pray for the Beis Hamikdash?
Why add in learning from Chamishah Asar b'Av, if not simply because the nights grow longer?
The man from Biala who chose right after Yom Kippur
The Rav says that one who feels he lacks yiras shamayim should know that Chamishah Asar b'Av is a time when it can be drawn.
The Rav says one must rejoice on Chamishah Asar b'Av that our avodah is precious to Hashem, and take strength from it.
The Rav says one must always pray for the rebuilding of the Beis Hamikdash and await it every day.
The Rav says that from Chamishah Asar b'Av one should add in Torah, in tefillah and in carefulness in every area of Yiddishkeit, grabbing the opportunity while it lasts.
